newsitem.title: FRANCE: French AIDS prosecutor urges clearing Fabius.
newsitem.headline: French AIDS prosecutor urges clearing Fabius.

text.p: A French special prosecutor investigating politicians' responsibility for a scandal over AIDS-tainted blood transfusions has recommended clearing former prime minister Laurent Fabius, his office said on Tuesday.

Prosecutor-general Jean-Francois Burgelin also found there was no case to answer against former health and social affairs ministers Edmond Herve and Georgina Dufoix in a report that outraged victims' families and lawyers.
All three Socialist politicians were in office when some 1,250 haemophiliacs were infected by blood products supplied by public health services in 1985. More than 400 have since died.
The investigation was conducted by the prosecutor of the Court of Justice of the Republic, a special body established to try ministers for offences committed while in office.

The three-judge court will now have to decide whether to follow his advice or send one or more of the ministers to trial on charges of being accomplices to poisoning, an offence which carries a maximum 30-year prison sentence.
"Convinced of serving the best interests of contemporary democracy, our response is to recommend that there is no case to answer," Burgelin wrote in the conclusion to his 380-page report.
He said he did not entirely rule out the ministers' responsibility for France's worst public health scandal but argued that theirs was political, not criminal, liability.

Fabius, 50, France's youngest prime minister in 1984-86, was seen as a potential presidential contender until the blood scandal overshadowed his career. He is now Socialist floor leader in the National Assembly.
"I find it revolting and offensive for the victims to ask to clear these ministers," said Joelle Bouchet, a mother of a child infected by tainted blood.
Max Lecoq, a lawyer for victims, also condemned the prosecutor. "The legal combat continues even if the dice are loaded by this procedure that favours ministers," he said.

Burgelin said Fabius may have been informed of problems involved in collecting blood supplies, and cast doubt over Fabius's statement that he knew nothing about the problems of non-treated blood products.
On a delay in approving tests for blood products, Burgelin simply noted Fabius's statement that he had acted "as soon as possible".

"Neither Mr Fabius nor Mr Herve had the medical knowledge which would have allowed them to understand the complex problem. These shortcomings may certainly imply a responsibility of the state but do not point to a penal responsibility of the ministers," Burgelin wrote.

Herve however was criticised for lack of initiative on tests, inaction on the lack of a ban on non-treated products and "strangely apathetic behaviour" as far as the delay in official approval for the tests was concerned.
Four senior public health officials were convicted of fraud in 1992 and given prison sentences of up to four years for knowingly allowing contaminated blood stocks to be given to haemophiliacs.
Their lawyers argued they had acted with the knowledge of the government, which delayed importing a U.S. blood-screening product to give French laboratories time to develop their own.
In a television interview, Dufoix said she felt "responsible but not guilty" -- a phrase used repeatedly by the French right to hound the Socialists from power in 1993.

The two men in charge of blood transfusions in 1985, Michel Garetta and Jean-Pierre Allain, both of whom were among those jailed, have since also been placed under investigation on the more serious charge of "poisoning".
